Mixed ingestion/query jobs and cold starts must not be confused with a homogeneous warm-query latency target. No unmeasured service-level promise is made.

Persistent corpus ingestion stores a checked FAISS/SQLite bundle through the same library used in experiments. Query requests retrieve candidates, then use the common selector and generator. Corpus IDs are constrained to simple names rather than arbitrary filesystem paths. This service is a local demonstration; its inference inputs contain no reference answers.

sections.title: Sampling, state preparation and a weak depth-one circuit
sections.text: Sampling, state preparation and a weak depth-one circuit

sections.title: Why a global phase cannot change an answer sample
sections.text:
Why a global phase cannot change an answer sample

A computational basis state corresponds to one exact binary subset. Write it as |x0>. The cost Hamiltonian is diagonal: H_C|x0> = E(x0)|x0>. Exponentiating this relation gives:


e^{-i\gamma H_C}|x_0\rangle=e^{-i\gamma E(x_0)}|x_0\rangle.


The multiplier has magnitude one and applies to the entire state. Measurement uses squared magnitudes, so multiplying every amplitude by that same complex number changes no probability. Applying a later linear mixer U_M cannot recover an observable difference:


U_M e^{-i\gamma H_C}|x_0\rangle=e^{-i\gamma E(x_0)}U_M|x_0\rangle.


Consequently, the frozen basis-start p=1 XY circuit has probabilities that depend on its mixer angle beta and starting subset, but not its first cost angle gamma. This gamma is a circuit angle, distinct from the graph-weight gamma in the selection objective. At p=2, mixing has created a superposition before the second cost layer, so the second cost angle can matter. The first remains inactive. This is an expressivity limitation, not a claim that QAOA generally ignores its objective. The classical optimizer still evaluates the expected energy under the chosen objective and can choose a different beta when that objective changes.

This diagnosis is verified in [the preparation regression check](../tests/test_preparation_control.py) by changing the first cost angle while holding the mixer angle fixed and comparing every state probability. The test then inserts feasible preparation and verifies that changing the cost angle does change probabilities, while all probability mass remains at the required count.

sections.title: Preparing a feasible superposition
sections.text:
Preparing a feasible superposition

The exploratory extension in [prepared_qaoa_study.py](../scripts/prepared_qaoa_study.py) keeps the original seeded subset but first applies one XY ring sweep at fixed angle pi/4. Every paired RXX/RYY exchange preserves the number of ones. Starting with k ones therefore produces a superposition of states that still have k ones. This is generally neither a uniform superposition nor a Dicke state.

If preparation produces sum_x c_x|x>, the cost layer produces sum_x c_x exp(-i gamma E(x))|x>. Different energies now receive different phases. A subsequent mixer can turn those relative phases into changed measurement probabilities through interference. This is the mechanism missing from the original first layer.

Preparation is not free: its gates, routing and depth are included when compiling the complete circuit. The fixed angle is not selected by looking for a favorable held-out answer result. This control is explicitly exploratory because the diagnosis occurred after the primary matrix was frozen. Both original and prepared results are retained. It would be misleading to silently replace the weaker implementation and describe the new outcome as the original principal experiment.

Generic compiled gate counts are also not lower bounds. A compiler that recognizes a known basis state could remove diagonal operations that only add a global phase. We report the actual fixed compiler policy and this limitation. Sparse symbolic interactions do not alone establish a necessary hardware cost reduction.

sections.title: How repeated samples can look like optimization
sections.text:
How repeated samples can look like optimization

Suppose one draw has probability u of being an optimal feasible subset. Independent draws miss every optimum with probability (1-u)^S. Therefore:


P(\text{at least one optimum})=1-(1-u)^S.


For uniform feasible sampling with one optimum among M subsets, u=1/M. With n=10 and k=5, M=10!/(5!5!)=252. At S=1,024, optimum coverage is approximately 0.9829. This is already high without a learned distribution. With n=16,k=5, M=4,368 and coverage is approximately 0.2090. A small exact-solver comparison can hide this distinction if it reports only the best of many samples.

Uniform feasible sampling is easy here: choose exactly k distinct indices uniformly, evaluate their objective, and keep the best. This baseline has no variational-angle training. QAOA's final 1,024 draws are additional to up to 64 objective evaluations used to choose angles. An equal-final-draw comparison is useful but is not equal-total-compute or a hardware speed comparison.

sections.title: Feasibility and expected best energy
sections.text:
Feasibility and expected best energy

Let F be the total single-draw probability on feasible subsets. Then the probability of obtaining no feasible subset in S draws is (1-F)^S. Ideal count-preserving execution gives F=1 up to numerical roundoff. A squared penalty gives no such finite-depth guarantee. We keep zero-feasible outcomes as failures; reporting only the successful subset of circuits would censor this cost.

To compute the expected best feasible energy, sort feasible states by energy e_1 <= ... <= e_M and let their raw probabilities be p_1,...,p_M. They sum to F and need not sum to one. Write C_j=sum from t=1 to j of p_t, with C_0=0. The probability that the best feasible sample has energy e_j is:


w_j=(1-C_{j-1})^S-(1-C_j)^S.


To see why, the first term says no sample has an energy smaller than e_j; the second removes the case where none has energy at most e_j either. Ties may be listed in any stable order because their energy is identical. These weights sum to 1-(1-F)^S, the chance of at least one feasible draw. Thus the conditional expected best energy is sum_j(e_jw_j) divided by 1-(1-F)^S. Subtracting the exact feasible optimum gives the conditional expected energy gap. The conditioning must be shown beside no-feasible probability so it does not hide failure risk.

The [sampling study](../scripts/sampling_coverage_study.py) evaluates these expressions using trained ideal statevectors on 20 real development-derived instances, four nested candidate sizes, two encodings and three seeds: 480 circuit solves. It uses no generated answers and no support labels. Floating-point probability sums are clipped to [0,1] at their numerical boundary, preventing an impossible negative failure probability of order 10^-15. The first numerical export is retained locally as an archive; this is a roundoff correction, not an outcome-based algorithm change.

sections.title: Reading statistical comparisons correctly
sections.text:
Reading statistical comparisons correctly

For question q, let d_q be method A's F1 minus method B's F1 after averaging each method's seeds. The estimated difference is the arithmetic mean of d_q across the N common questions. A paired bootstrap samples N question IDs with replacement, recomputes that mean, and repeats 10,000 times. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles give the reported 95% interval. Pairing preserves the fact that both methods face the same easy or difficult question.

If three seeds on one question score 1, 0.5 and 0, that question contributes 0.5. It does not become three independently sampled questions. If the last seed fails, its F1 remains zero and the mean is still 0.5. In contrast, missing resource measurements remain missing: inventing a gate count of zero for an unexecuted circuit would also bias a resource mean. Completed circuits with measured zero feasibility do contribute their actual zero.

An interval entirely above zero supports a positive difference under this sample and analysis. An interval spanning zero leaves both positive and negative effects plausible. It does not establish that the methods are equal. Noninferiority would require a chosen acceptable loss and a suitable interval bound declared before looking at the result. This project does not retrospectively invent such a tolerance.

The question is the resampling unit, but source passages and compositional question templates can still be shared across questions. The bootstrap does not model every such cluster. The two generators are from one family, and numerical simulator training is not physical-device execution. These limits restrict generalization even when a difference looks clear. Secondary exploratory tables are not a large collection of independent confirmatory discoveries.

sections.title: Artifact checks and independent reconstruction
sections.text:
Artifact checks and independent reconstruction

A result is traceable when a table cell can be followed to question scores, predictions, selected IDs, objective coefficients and the exact code/configuration that produced them. Checksums detect changed bytes; they do not establish scientific correctness. The [final auditor](../scripts/audit_final_runs.py) additionally recomputes answer scores, source membership, count/token constraints and pair-sum energies, and retokenizes saved prompts against pinned tokenizers. A failed invariant stops assembly rather than silently correcting a scientific record.

Compact public predictions omit large prompts and parameter traces but preserve the fields needed to regenerate tables, with a SHA-256 digest of their compressed file. [Public-table reconstruction](../scripts/reproduce_public_tables.py) needs neither model weights nor raw dataset text. This tests statistical reconstruction from released outcomes; it is different from rerunning retrieval, selection and generation. Full local artifacts and split/corpus restoration scripts support that more expensive route.

For numbers that are mathematically equivalent but differ slightly in floating-point reduction order on another machine, reconstruction accepts an absolute/relative tolerance of 10^-12. It still requires identical structure, IDs, counts and file hashes. Tolerance is not permission to substitute different predictions.

sections.title: A container image and a dependency lock solve different problems
sections.text:
A container image and a dependency lock solve different problems

A lock records exact package versions. An image packages an installed operating-system/runtime filesystem. Pinning the base-image digest fixes its bytes, while pinning runtime dependencies prevents a rebuild from silently adopting newer libraries. Neither fixes the host kernel, CPU/GPU hardware or every external driver. The CPU service and CUDA experiments deliberately have different environment snapshots; passing a CPU service check is not evidence of bit-identical GPU outputs.

The container runs as a nonroot user, mounts weights read-only and stores mutable indexes/jobs in a separate named volume. This separates immutable inputs from runtime state. Removing a disposable container need not remove that named volume. Restart recovery can then distinguish completed jobs from interrupted ones. These mechanisms are useful in other model services even when no quantum component exists.

Correctness tests also have dependency boundaries. The lightweight workflow checks the available baseline contracts and explicitly skips integrations whose optional packages are absent. The fuller research workflow installs Qiskit/FAISS/service dependencies and executes those integrations. A skip is visible absence of a check, not a passed execution; the full suite currently has 46 tests. Testing source spectra, feasibility and probability sensitivity with actual Qiskit is different from exercising HTTP state transitions with an explicitly labeled fake inference engine.

sections.title: Connecting the completed results to the mathematics
sections.text:
Connecting the completed results to the mathematics

The principal evidence-minus-magnitude differences are -0.0363 and -0.0095 F1, with intervals that cross zero. This does not prove that entity links are always useless. It says this extractor, scoring rule, sparsifier, shallow circuit, candidate pool and sample do not establish the proposed benefit. A weak feature, limited statistical precision and an optimization restriction can all matter; the current experiment does not independently identify their causal shares.

The prepared control removes the specific global-phase degeneracy, but its two evidence-guidance intervals still cross zero. An improvement in expressivity is a mathematical property; an improvement in answer F1 is an empirical property. They must be measured separately. The full report retains both controls rather than replacing one after seeing scores.

For a complete optimum, E(x) <= E(x) for every feasible x under that coefficient array. This inequality contains no reference answer, supporting annotation or LLM likelihood. It therefore cannot imply that the generated answer is correct. The released error analysis demonstrates real cases of lower common energy and lower answer F1. It evaluates the relevance subset using the same full coefficients, avoiding the invalid comparison of energies from different graph weights.

A 1,200-token cap bounds formatted context but leaves room for different consumption and selected counts. Comparing it with a 500-question count result would additionally change the question population, since the token condition has 100 questions. Within-condition paired comparisons are interpretable; a raw cross-table difference does not isolate the effect of the cap. Larger candidate pools similarly change retrieval opportunities and optimization cost together.

The gate-cap diagnostic uses descending recorded floating-point fractions and an integer floor edge budget. Near a floating-point boundary, a value represented as 0.3999999999999999 can retain 17 of 45 edges rather than the 18 associated with an exact decimal 0.4. The artifact records the actual fraction, retained indices, trial costs and final circuit. The principal 0.5 fractions are exactly representable and unaffected. Final cap validation, not a rounded display label, establishes feasibility. Compiled gate cost is not monotonic in retained edges because routing and optimization can change.

The service measures an entire three-method comparison request, not a single generated token or one selector in isolation. Its p95 comes from only five repeated fictional requests. Batching measurements use synchronized GPU embedding operations on 128 fixed chunks; their scope differs from both the CPU service and dataset evaluation. An engineering number becomes useful when its workload, denominator, warm/cold state and resource conditions are explicit.

The 110 frozen optimization instances allow Qiskit/MILP experiments without loading an embedding model, raw dataset or generator. Reference solver optima in that bundle are analysis outputs, not answer annotations. The reproduction command passes only coefficients and constraints to the solver, then compares its output against the stored execution. Reconstructing saved statistical tables, rerunning a solver on fixed features, and rerunning end-to-end RAG are three different levels of reproduction.

sections.title: Turning numerical artifacts into a manuscript
sections.text:
Turning numerical artifacts into a manuscript

The report assembler reads completed per-question outcomes, derives statistics and fills only named numerical blocks in the manuscript. This keeps the explanation editable while avoiding hand-transcribed table values. The PDF renderer typesets equations, tables and generated figures from that source. A successful rendering process can still produce clipped labels, split captions or unreadable columns, so each of the 13 pages was separately rasterized and visually inspected.

An export checksum identifies the reviewed PDF bytes. It does not establish that the research is correct or guarantee a bit-identical export with different fonts or rendering-library versions. Similarly, a polished PDF is not a submitted or accepted publication. Source review, author responsibility, venue requirements and independent evidence checking remain distinct from layout QA.

sections.title: Why the paired XY gates preserve passage count
sections.text:
Why the paired XY gates preserve passage count

The Pauli X operator exchanges |0> and |1>. For a pair of qubits, XX sends |01> to |10> and |00> to |11>. YY also sends |01> to |10>, but sends |00> to -|11>. Adding XX and YY therefore cancels the changes between |00> and |11>, while retaining exchange between |01> and |10>. Exchange moves a selected bit to another position without changing how many are selected.

Qiskit's paired RXX(beta) and RYY(beta) rotations on the same edge commute and multiply to exp[-i beta(XX+YY)/2]. On the one-selected-bit subspace this gives:


|01\rangle\longmapsto\cos(\beta)|01\rangle-i\sin(\beta)|10\rangle.


At beta=pi/4, those two local probabilities are both one half. A sweep across overlapping ring edges is not a uniform distribution over every k-subset, because adjacent edge operations do not generally commute. Each edge nevertheless preserves total count, so their composition does too. The diagonal cost layer also preserves count. This explains ideal feasibility without requiring a penalty. Physical noise that flips bits can break the property, as the separate noisy development diagnostic demonstrates.

sections.title: Versioned release versus scientific acceptance
sections.text:
Versioned release versus scientific acceptance

A source archive records one committed tree; a wheel installs its Python packages; a PDF is a readable rendered account; checksums identify the supplied bytes. These objects serve different consumers. The release builder checks their consistency and rejects accidental inclusion of datasets, weights or private notes. Public availability still does not supply an unspecified license, establish novelty or replace peer review. The project therefore separates a reproducible software/research artifact from the human decisions and external publication process.

sections.title: Dashboard foundations — state, rendering and local assets
sections.text: Dashboard foundations — state, rendering and local assets The dashboard is a client of the existing service, not another retrieval or solver implementation. [HTML](../src/qrag_service/static/index.html) describes its headings, form controls and result containers. [CSS](../src/qrag_service/static/dashboard.css) controls spacing, typography, color, grids and narrower-screen layouts. [JavaScript](../src/qrag_service/static/dashboard.js) keeps inputs synchronized, submits requests, polls jobs and renders responses. Separating these files makes their responsibilities easier to inspect. [The service](../src/qrag_service/app.py) serves their files under /assets; the wheel includes them and the local fonts. A page that works from source but omits these files from its wheel would be an incomplete installation. The request sequence is: edit question/sources → validate the input shape → POST the comparison JSON → receive HTTP 202 with a job ID → poll the status URL → render completed results or the reported failure. HTTP acceptance is not successful inference. The browser disables editing during a comparison so the displayed request cannot change underneath a running job. A finalization block restores controls after success or failure. Editing after completion labels the visible answers as results of the previous input. Source cards and JSON are two views of the same array. Editing a card updates the serialized JSON; switching back from JSON validates and rebuilds the cards. IDs stay stable unless explicitly edited in JSON. Removing a source lowers the count limit, and the count cannot exceed the available pool or ten. These are interface checks for understandable errors; Pydantic still validates requests independently on the server. A client-side check cannot protect an API from another client that bypasses the page. Rendering untrusted source titles, text and answers uses DOM textContent rather than interpreting them as HTML. For example, the literal answer remains text instead of becoming an image element with an event handler. The DOM check verifies this behavior on that fixture. This addresses HTML interpretation at the rendering boundary; it does not prove that the generator resists malicious instructions inside its context or establish comprehensive application security. The interface is a small state machine: idle, submitting/queued/running, completed, failed, or inputs changed since the displayed result. Model readiness is separate: a cold service can accept a job that loads weights. A simulated quantum result is labeled simulated; a permitted classical fallback identifies the actual method. Result cards show the supplied context, not verified causal citations. The study totals and illustrative hero diagram are kept separate from live results so visual presentation does not invent measurements. Self-hosted fonts mean the browser requests font bytes from the same local service. It does not contact a third-party font service at page load. Font files remain separate upstream works with their included licenses. Responsive CSS changes grid columns and type sizes at narrower widths; reduced-motion settings disable nonessential animation. Keyboard tabs, visible focus styles, labels and live status text support interaction, but their presence alone is not an accessibility certification. Verification has distinct layers. Node checks JavaScript syntax. jsdom executes DOM/event behavior with synthetic API responses but does not lay out the CSS. FastAPI tests verify file routes and request contracts. Wheel inspection verifies distribution contents. Real local HTTP inference verifies the model/solver integration. A browser screenshot and interactive desktop/mobile review would verify rendered layout; that last layer remained blocked by browser-control errors during this revision. None of these interface checks changes or improves the scientific objective or measured answer scores.

sections.title: Interactive walkthrough mathematics and content provenance
sections.text:
Interactive walkthrough mathematics and content provenance

The project journey at /journey explains the existing research through locally computed examples and views of saved artifacts. The [editorial content](journey/content.cjs) supplies the narrative; the [compiler](../scripts/build_journey.cjs) incorporates full public references and unchanged numerical JSON. The [client](../src/qrag_service/static/journey.js) computes the illustrative examples below. These are not alternative research implementations, model predictions or quantum hardware runs.

sections.title: 1. A valid vector example for subset energy
sections.text:
1. A valid vector example for subset energy

Let the normalized question vector be (1,0), and passage vectors be A=(0.8,0.6), B=(0.6,0.8), C=(0.6,−0.8). Each has length one because its squared components sum to one. Dot products with the question give relevance (0.8,0.6,0.6). Pairwise cosine values are A·B=0.96, A·C=0, B·C=−0.28. Clipping negative redundancy to zero yields pair scores (0.96,0,0). These numbers come from a consistent geometry rather than independently invented similarity arrays.

With exactly two passages, relevance weight one, redundancy weight β=0.5 and evidence weight zero, the three feasible energies are A+B=−0.8−0.6+0.5×0.96=−0.92, A+C=−1.40, B+C=−1.20. Thus relevance-only ranking chooses A+B while this toy objective chooses A+C. Add illustrative complementarity values C_AC=0.8 and C_BC=0.2; with γ=1, A+C becomes −1.40−0.8=−2.20. This demonstrates a coefficient's effect on selection. It establishes neither useful semantic evidence nor better generated answers.

sections.title: 2. MILP products and the relaxation boundary
sections.text:
2. MILP products and the relaxation boundary

For binary x and z, impose 0≤y≤1, y≤x, y≤z, y≥x+z−1. If either input is zero, the upper bound and nonnegativity force y=0. If both are one, the last bound and upper bounds force y=1. Therefore continuous y equals the binary product. In general its allowed interval is [max(0,x+z−1), min(x,z)]. If both inputs are relaxed to 0.5, the interval becomes [0,0.5], which includes values other than the true product 0.25. Exactness depends on binary inputs; the linear relaxation has a different meaning.

sections.title: 3. A two-bit Ising identity
sections.text:
3. A two-bit Ising identity

The displayed energy is E=−x₀−0.5x₁+0.2x₀x₁. Substitute x=(1−z)/2. Expanding the product gives 0.05(1−z₀−z₁+z₀z₁). Combining constants gives −0.5−0.25+0.05=−0.7; combining linear coefficients gives 0.5−0.05=0.45 and 0.25−0.05=0.20. Thus H=−0.7+0.45z₀+0.20z₁+0.05z₀z₁. For x=(1,1), z=(−1,−1) and both energies equal −1.30. The example uses qubit zero as the least significant bit and preserves the constant when comparing energies.

For the density illustration, expand λ(Σxᵢ−k)². Since binary xᵢ²=xᵢ, it contributes λ(1−2k) to every linear coefficient, 2λ to every unordered pair and constant λk². At n=10 there are 10×9/2=45 possible pairs. Retaining half by a floor rule leaves 22 semantic pairs; the generic squared penalty still adds interactions on all 45. Exact cancellation can be an exception, and this pair count is not a compiled gate count. XY mixing avoids that penalty but has its own costs.

sections.title: 4. Global phase versus useful relative phase
sections.text:
4. Global phase versus useful relative phase

The two-state illustration uses basis vectors |10⟩ and |01⟩, energies −1 and −0.5, and mixer exp(−iβX) within this one-excitation subspace. Starting with amplitudes (u,v), the cost layer gives a=u exp(iγ) and b=v exp(iγ/2). The mixer gives final amplitudes cos(β)a−i sin(β)b and cos(β)b−i sin(β)a; squared magnitudes give the displayed probabilities and sum to one.

For a basis start, (u,v)=(1,0), so the probabilities are cos²β and sin²β, independent of γ. Its initial cost phase is global. For the prepared toy, (u,v)=(1/√2,1/√2), the relative phase can change interference and therefore probabilities. The research preparation is generally nonuniform and uses the full recorded ansatz; this exact two-state calculation teaches the mechanism without claiming to rerun that ansatz.

sections.title: 5. Sparsification and solver error are separate
sections.text:
5. Sparsification and solver error are separate

The six-variable example has nine signed edges and k=3, hence 20 feasible selections. A retained-fraction slider uses the hard budget floor(f×9) and four displayed ranking rules. The random-style toy uses a fixed order; the research rule uses recorded random seeds. Removed absolute mass is δ=Σ_removed|bᵢⱼ|. A returned point is required to lie within ε of the sparse optimum. Comparing its full energy against the full optimum illustrates the already derived bound full gap≤2δ+ε. The client enumerates all 20 feasible states, so the toy can display both optima exactly. It does not certify answer quality, and enumerating a toy does not demonstrate quantum speedup. The main sparsification section above provides the general proof and assumptions.

sections.title: 6. Sampling coverage and its assumptions
sections.text:
6. Sampling coverage and its assumptions

There are M=binomial(n,k) feasible fixed-count subsets. Under independent uniform sampling, the chance of missing one designated optimum in a draw is 1−1/M; missing it S times is (1−1/M)^S. Therefore coverage is 1−(1−1/M)^S. For n=10,k=5, M=252, S=1024, coverage is about 98.29%. For n=16,k=5, M=4368 and coverage is about 20.90%. Multiple optima increase coverage; correlated or nonuniform draws require a different model. Best-of-many uniform sampling is a meaningful baseline in a tiny feasible space, not proof of favorable scaling.

sections.title: 7. Reading the measured charts
sections.text:
7. Reading the measured charts

Charts use the saved JSON tables rather than toy outputs. Answer F1 uses a shared zero-to-one axis. Failed records contribute zero to the reported answer denominator. Successful-only token summaries are labelled, and complete-circuit means disclose their own denominator. Seed repetitions are not treated as extra independent questions. Paired confidence intervals describe differences between methods on common questions; an interval crossing zero does not establish a positive benefit. Main and prepared conditions remain explicitly separate. None of these chart controls starts a fresh experiment.

sections.title: 8. Deterministic content is a reproducibility contract
sections.text:
8. Deterministic content is a reproducibility contract

An explicit allowlist defines what may enter the browser bundle. The compiler renders Markdown with raw HTML disabled, renders trusted math at build time, rewrites public reference links to the in-site reader, and packages local figures, fonts and licenses. SHA-256 hashes identify the exact source bytes; a hash proves identity, not scientific truth. The manifest also identifies editorial/compiler/tool-lock inputs. CI rebuilds and checks for differences so stale documentation cannot silently remain in a supposedly current bundle.

The browser reads one local content bundle and manipulates its own DOM. It inserts search queries and artifact JSON as text. It does not need a model or Node runtime. Guided/deep modes expose the same information at different initial expansion levels. Automatic visual motion respects reduced-motion settings. Numerical tests check the equations, DOM checks check events, HTTP tests check cold-engine asset serving, and wheel inspection checks packaging. None substitutes for real-browser painting or independent scientific evaluation. The [journey guide](journey/README.md) and [verification receipt](research_report/evidence/journey_20261112.json) separate these layers.

documents.title: Development sequence
documents.html:
Development sequence and implementation decisions

Version 1.4 working edition | Updated November 12 2026

This document records the progression from the exploratory prototype through the current research implementation. The first baseline was implemented during one November 4 session; its dependency-ordered account comes first. The November 10 phase entries then record the larger data, retrieval, optimization, quantum, service and research work. Early status tables are labeled historical and do not override later measured progress.

The progress report records outcomes. Technical foundations supplies derivations and worked examples.

Current state after the full local run

This is the current summary. The stages and dated checkpoints below preserve what was true during implementation; their “remaining,” “next” and “pending” statements are historical unless repeated here.

Phase Implemented and executed Remaining boundary
A Measured environment, protocol, literature comparison, locks, manifests and CI Exhaustive novelty certification and independent scientific review are not established.
B Two frozen splits, annotation-preserving adapters, official metric checks and real empty/oracle diagnostics Known contamination and annotation limitations remain.
C Token-safe chunks, persistent embedding/graph caches, checked FAISS/SQLite index and retrieval/reranking policies Cache and retrieval profiles are workload-specific, not general latency guarantees.
D Signed count/token MILP, exhaustive checks, heuristics and entity-link features Independent graph annotation and original-model closest-method reproduction are unfinished.
E Actual QAOA simulations, mappings, sampling, noise diagnostic and full compilation No physical quantum execution or quantum token-budget encoding.
F Four hard-budget sparsifiers, development calibration and ablations The proposed guidance benefit and preserved answer quality were not established.
G 18 primary conditions plus six scoped controls, audited outcomes and reconstructed statistics Small quantum subsets, shared generator family and non-certified large MILP cases limit generalization.
H Numerical manuscript, reviewed 13-page PDF, real-model service/container checks and batch profiling No independent causal error annotation, browser visual review or demo video; no production deployment claim.
I Source/wheel/PDF/checksum preview release and reproduction instructions Independent review, authorship/rights decisions, venue formatting and submission remain outstanding.

There are 53,230 method/question records across 24 runs, covering 1,000 distinct held-out questions with methods, seeds and generators repeated. Of these records, 53,209 succeeded and 21 failed; failures remain in answer averages. The exact core source is preserved in the scientific snapshot. The final audit, complete result index and claim map connect status to evidence.

The original-plan coverage assessment lists adaptations and unfinished requirements explicitly. Local phase completion is not literal completion of every original plan item, publication acceptance or completion of interactive learning exercises.

Historical baseline sequence — November 4–9

The next eight stages describe the first working slice. Their limitations motivated later phases and do not replace the current summary above.

Starting point before the baseline

The prototype already had processed HotpotQA subsets, MiniLM retrieval, a relevance–redundancy QUBO, classical exact optimization, a local generator and a QAOA wrapper.

Its principal evaluation used the classical solver and measured selected-document quality. It did not evaluate generated answers. Its unconstrained optimizer could select more documents than top-five ranking, so higher recall could not establish a better selection policy at equal context size.

The objective was retained as a starting model, while the evaluation and execution contracts were rebuilt.

Stage one explicit data and configuration contracts

Added: data.py, config.py, configuration, and package metadata.

The source JSON is adapted into separate QueryInput and EvaluationLabels objects. IDs, titles, text and questions are validated; gold fields do not reach the normal inference interface. Configuration makes weights, seed, model revisions, limits and short-pool behavior explicit.

Why this came first: every later comparison depends on knowing its inputs and settings. A selector that can inspect reference labels or inherit hidden script constants cannot support a reliable experiment.

Remaining at this stage: source-sentence offsets, full duplicate checks and frozen fresh evaluation partitions. The dependency lock then covered only the core numeric pair rather than the complete model stack. Phases A–C subsequently added the broader environment, data and retrieval contracts.

Stage two answer and evidence metrics

Added: metrics.py.

Answer exact match and token F1 are calculated separately from document precision, recall and complete-support coverage. Reference-normalization fixtures include repeated words, punctuation and special answers.

Why: document selection is an intermediate task. The project needs generated-answer measurements before claiming that a selection improvement benefits RAG.

Verification: offline metric fixtures and the later real generation run. Semantic near-matches and annotation inconsistencies remain visible in error analysis.

Stage three a common objective and controlled classical selection

Added: optimization.py.

SelectionProblem stores one linear vector and a strict upper-triangular interaction matrix. An exact-count constraint prevents the optimizer from improving recall merely by choosing more passages.

The module implements stable relevance top-k, MILP with product linearization, and a tiny exhaustive oracle. SelectionResult distinguishes ranking, optimal and limited outcomes and retains bounds when available.

Why: formulation and solver effects must be separable. A tested energy evaluator also gives the future quantum mapping a reference independent of circuit software.

Verification: MILP agrees with exhaustive enumeration on tiny positive/negative-pair cases and count boundaries. Tests also cover time-limited solutions without falsely labeling them optimal.

Remaining at this stage: native token constraints and additional classical baselines, subsequently implemented in Phase D.

Stage four common real-model adapters

Added: models.py.

The model adapter resolves immutable MiniLM/Qwen snapshots, loads once, produces shared per-question features, constructs a consistent chat prompt and generates actual short answers. Embedding overlength and generation-prompt overflow fail explicitly by default.

Why: the compared selectors must use the same models and prompt policy. Model loading, feature generation and answer generation are distinct timing stages.

Remaining at this stage: chunking, persistent embedding reuse, hardware profiling and generation diagnostics with empty or oracle evidence, subsequently covered by Phases A–C and the final service/batching checks.

Stage five experiment orchestration and artifact integrity

Added: runner and artifact handling.

Each question is scored once; both methods consume the same candidate pool and features. Selected context uses original candidate order. Labels are applied only after selection/generation.

The runner saves manifests, question-level JSONL records and summaries. The manifest identifies data bytes, qrag source files, models, settings and runtime. Atomic writes and guarded resume prevent partial files and accidental mixing of incompatible runs.

Why: an aggregate result without the predictions and settings behind it cannot explain what changed or support a reproducibility check.

Historical runner boundary: completed error records are retained and skipped on resume. The later main-study journal retries errors with explicit attempt numbers while protecting successful keys. Failures before a run store exists may still have only a CLI error; not every possible startup failure produces a manifest.

Stage six independent correctness and package checks

Added: offline tests, an editable package and CI configuration.

The seventeen test methods exercise contracts and mathematics without downloading language models. An explicitly labeled fake backend tests orchestration; it is unavailable as an experimental CLI mode.

The package installed locally without downloads. No completed remote CI run was claimed at this stage; later phase entries record actual GitHub executions.

Why: a real model can produce plausible answers while masking a wrong objective or metric. Mathematical and interface checks need independent expected outcomes.

Stage seven the real development run

Experiment date: November 4 2026. Run: baseline_dev_001.

MiniLM and Qwen ran locally on CPU with four PyTorch threads. There were three development questions and two methods per question. All six records succeeded with exactly five selected passages and no recorded embedding truncation or output-limit hit.

Both methods obtained answer EM/F1 of 0.3333. MILP obtained lower energy on each instance and higher average annotated document recall. Context-token consumption differed, so this was a fixed-count experiment rather than a token-matched comparison.

What this established: the complete baseline execution path works and exposes optimization, evidence and answer quality as different measurements.

What remains unestablished: general superiority, statistical significance, corpus-scale retrieval benefits, a novel graph method and a quantum advantage.

Stage eight audit and objective documentation

Documentation and audit date: November 9 2026.

The saved objective energies and answer/evidence metrics were recomputed against the recorded coefficients and unchanged references. Dataset and qrag source hashes matched the saved run. The seventeen offline tests passed again.

One question had a semantic near-match rejected by token scoring. Another asked for a film but recorded a person as its answer; the earlier investigation located the same inconsistency in the cached upstream record. Neither primary label nor scoring rule was silently altered.

Added the objective progress report, compact evidence snapshot and detailed companion. No new model inference result is implied by this documentation work.

Decisions and alternatives

Decision Reason Consequence or limitation
Use supplied pools first Isolates context selection Does not evaluate corpus search
Separate labels in data objects Reduces accidental answer leakage Still requires split and contamination checks
Start with exact-count budgets Removes passage-count imbalance Token lengths remain unequal
Use native MILP count constraints Gives a strong checkable classical reference Quantum encodings still require separate work
Use continuous product auxiliaries Exact with binary original variables The continuous relaxation allows more points
Keep original context ordering Controls a generation variable Order sensitivity remains an experimental question
Fail overlong inputs visibly Avoids hidden representation loss Chunking is required for larger runs
Use JSON artifacts before tracking infrastructure Keeps individual outcomes auditable Rich experiment dashboards remain later work
Preserve problematic references in primary scoring Avoids result-driven label changes Annotation errors must be reported separately

Historical status after the first baseline

Phase Status at the first-baseline checkpoint Gap at that checkpoint
A reproducibility and research protocol Partial Literature matrix, contribution assessment, fuller profiling and full dependency lock
B data and answer evaluation Partial Fresh frozen splits, source mappings and diagnostic experiments
C retrieval and caching Started Chunking, cache, index, retrieval baselines and token-budget mode
D classical optimization and evidence model Partial Other classical selectors, token constraints and graph features
E QAOA integration and resources Pending beyond legacy wrapper Shared-problem quantum experiments and full cost accounting
F candidate sparsification method Pending Method, generic comparisons and development ablations
G frozen evaluation Pending Multi-dataset controlled runs and uncertainty analysis
H manuscript and demonstration Pending beyond progress documentation Complete paper, research figures and demonstration
I submission package Pending Reviewed manuscript and reproducible release

At this checkpoint, no complete formal phase A–I was claimed merely because the first working baseline existed. The current summary at the top records subsequent work.

Dependency sequence recorded after the first baseline

  1. Complete the structured prior-work comparison and make the novelty hypothesis explicit.
  2. Finalize data provenance, frozen splits and diagnostic evaluation.
  3. Add token-aware chunking, source mappings and persistent embedding caching.
  4. Implement token-budget selection and additional classical comparisons.
  5. Add graph-derived features and evaluate their contribution classically.
  6. Integrate QAOA with the same problems, constraints and resource reporting.
  7. Evaluate the candidate sparsifier before freezing final experiments.

The implementation plan contains the full backlog. Updating this sequence should record what actually changed, why it changed and which artifact verifies it, rather than marking work complete because a planned date has passed.

November 10, 2026 — Phase A execution foundation

  1. Re-read the plan and current inference, solver and artifact contracts. The working tree was clean at execution start.
  2. Verified the now-visible GPU, executed tensor/HiGHS/quantum checks, and preserved the earlier CPU experiment as historical evidence.
  3. Installed the missing testing/service tools in the project virtual environment and recorded the exact installed dependency graph. No system Python or driver change was made.
  4. Checked 19 primary research sources, distinguishing close-method inspection from abstract-level context. Recorded reproduction limits instead of claiming to have reproduced unavailable original settings.
  5. Froze a protocol separating graph, sparsification and solver questions. Actual sample sizes will be chosen from development timing before held-out evaluation.

Verification: 17 baseline tests passed; dependency consistency check passed. New evidence: environment report. This phase establishes the research/execution foundation; it does not finish data preparation or demonstrate an empirical method benefit. Next dependency: trustworthy dataset partitions and annotation-preserving data contracts.

November 10, 2026 — Phase B data and evaluation

Extended the existing immutable data contracts without passing labels into inference. Added official-format HotpotQA and MuSiQue-Ans adapters, sentence validation, paragraph identities, aliases and dataset-specific answer scoring. Prepared fresh frozen splits from primary sources before any new held-out model run. Downloaded only public data/model artifacts; no paid compute was used.

Verified the scoring implementation against 1,004 pairs per official evaluator, plus four new data-contract tests. All 21 offline tests pass. Executed six real GPU generations to establish empty/gold diagnostic paths and preservation of actual prompt IDs. The diagnostic is separate from the main benchmark and is not a claim of equal-budget quality improvement.

The split preparation script refuses to overwrite existing frozen output. Its source revisions, IDs and hashes enable later reconstruction. Remaining independence limits include paraphrases, common source documents and unknown model pretraining data. Next dependency: token-safe representations, persistent caches, retrieval and explicit budget handling.

November 10, 2026 — Phase C retrieval foundation

Implemented token-aware source-preserving chunks first, then reused their exact text in the cache, dense scoring, index and reranker. This order prevents caching a silently truncated representation. Added immutable FAISS/SQLite bundles, lexical scores and rank fusion. The cross-encoder's paired input length is checked with its own tokenizer, because another model's safe input is not automatically safe for it.

The first real profile encoded 534 chunks plus 50 questions: 584 misses, followed by 584 hits on repetition. Encoding time fell from 1.587 to 0.296 seconds under this measured condition. Index restoration returned identical results. Twenty-five offline tests pass. Two initial retrieval-test expectations were corrected before this milestone: reciprocal-rank fusion is nonlinear in rank, and an intentionally tiny test chunk needed an appropriately small overlap.

No answer-quality conclusion follows from this profile. Native token constraints and comparable generated-answer runs remain coupled to Phase D's solver work. Full corpus evaluation comes later after the common candidate construction is frozen.

November 10, 2026 — Phase D optimization and first broad pilot

Extended the common problem with optional linear token costs, a variable-count mode and minimum count. Retained the original exact-k API for historical tests. Added independent budget validation and exhaustive comparisons on small signed objectives. Added feasible heuristics before integrating graph coefficients so objective changes and solver changes remain separable.

Built the graph from permitted text and question inputs only; stored exact mention spans and named the result an entity-link graph. Added cached extraction and explicit limitations. Integrated shared candidates, token-safe embeddings, classical comparators, full source snapshots and compact exports in a new study runner while retaining the historical baseline entry point.

Executed 500 fixed-count development records (50 questions by 10 methods) and 100 token-budget records (10 by 10). All completed successfully; actual token caps were independently checked. The first graph weight worsened mean answer F1 relative to the base objective. That result is retained, and no graph improvement is claimed. Twenty-nine offline tests pass. Independent graph annotation and original-model prior reproduction remain limitations. Next dependency: exact quantum mapping, actual QAOA sampling and complete compiled-resource accounting.

November 10, 2026 — Phase E integrated quantum experiments

Implemented the Ising map and exhaustive spectrum checks before QAOA. Added both dense cardinality penalties and a seeded count-preserving XY ring, then exact-expectation/finite-shot training and explicit final-sample selection. Added complete-circuit compilation on common synthetic targets and an optional final-measurement noise model.

Executed 140 records on 10 development questions with two depths, two mixers and three seeds, plus a shot-training control. Executed a separate nine-record noise diagnostic on three questions after label-independent relevance reduction to eight candidates. All records completed successfully. Thirty-two offline tests pass. Observed that ideal feasibility and compiled cost trade off: XY preserves count but is costlier for these dense instances; synthetic noise substantially reduces its measured feasibility. No hardware or speedup claim is made.

The next dependency is sparsification: retain a declared number of interactions, compare against generic rules, and always evaluate selected contexts under the original full target. Any claimed savings must survive the constraint encoding and compilation just measured.

November 10, 2026 — Phase F development decisions and sparsification

Implemented all four hard-budget sparsifiers and checked signs, masks and the elementary full-energy bound against exhaustive optima. Added a best-of-feasible-random-samples control because the quantum policy also evaluates many measured candidates. Added paired question-level analysis and tests preventing seed repeats from becoming artificial sample size.

Ran 1,400 calibration records across 200 development questions, selecting gamma=0.2 before held-out evaluation. Ran 900 sparsification/encoding development records across 30 questions. The results support a compiler/encoding effect but not a reliable superiority claim for evidence guidance. Continued the study as a controlled comparison, retaining unfavorable outcomes and original settings.

Replaced quadratic-cost artifact rewrites for the new study runner with a durable append journal and explicit retry semantics; the legacy runner remains historically compatible. Added a restore-by-manifest script and verified all four dataset hashes after independent reconstruction. Thirty-eight offline tests pass. Next: freeze the complete evaluation matrix, run new held-out questions, quantify paired uncertainty, then write the manuscript around observed findings.

November 10, 2026 — Phase G freeze checkpoint

Added bounded-corpus retrieval and explicit evaluation of missing support, then constructed the common candidate files before answer generation. Added memory high-water marks and stage timing fields. Formatted and linted the Python sources and reran all 39 tests before freezing the final configurations. Completed a separate Qwen 3B GPU smoke and a 16-candidate development quantum profile. The frozen matrix is now ready for execution; no held-out result is claimed at this checkpoint.

Phase G restart: provenance invariant repair

A real held-out input revealed the Unicode surface/canonical distinction. Stopped the matrix, retained the complete first run and partial subsequent run, reproduced the assertion from the source text, added a targeted regression, and restarted every condition with unchanged scientific settings. Forty-five tests pass. The first cycle remains an auditable superseded implementation run, not a pool from which favorable results are chosen.

Phase H parallel preparation while frozen runs execute

Placed the API in a separate package so service changes do not alter the frozen research source fingerprint. Implemented input validation, bounded jobs, persistence, readiness, fallback accounting, corpus ingestion/query and local tracing. Built and started the full CPU container, verified HTTP endpoints and checked read-only access to the pinned model snapshots. The browser inventory is empty, so visual UI review is not claimed. Prepared the manuscript source and PDF renderer, deferring numerical claims until the full results exist.

Phase G diagnostic extension — check what a shallow circuit can express

Added an answer-free development mechanism study rather than interpreting the final best-of-1,024 sample alone. It trains 480 circuits across 20 questions and nested sizes, then computes optimum coverage and expected best feasible energy directly from each ideal distribution. The first export exposed a roughly 10^-15 negative no-feasible probability from normalization roundoff; clamped probability sums at their mathematical [0,1] boundary, retained the initial local export, and regenerated the diagnostic. No scoring coefficients or training policy changed.

The result prompted an analytic circuit check: the original first cost layer acts on a basis state and is a global phase. Confirmed this by varying the angle and comparing complete probability vectors. Added a regression showing that a fixed feasible preparation sweep makes the first cost angle observable while preserving count. This was a mathematical diagnosis, not a search for a favorable answer score.

Kept every original frozen condition. Added separately hashed, explicitly exploratory prepared-circuit configurations, with one fixed pi/4 XY ring sweep before cost evolution. Archived extension source separately and included its hash in the study identity. This avoids changing the core while original experiments are active and makes the difference reproducible. The forthcoming analysis must compare the original and prepared circuits, disclose the post-freeze scope, and include preparation costs. Forty-six correctness tests are now defined; the new mathematical regression passes.

Prepared independent final artifact audits, compressed prediction exports, restoration of all six corpus-candidate files and model-free table reconstruction. The restored corpus inputs matched their frozen hashes exactly. Circuit summaries include measured zero-feasibility failures, preventing a successful-only denominator from overstating feasibility. Final answer comparison assembly remains dependent on completion of the frozen runs.

Phase H packaging checkpoint — keep installation evidence separate

Captured and pinned the observed CPU container dependencies rather than assuming the CUDA laptop lock was portable. Rebuilt the image, started a nonroot instance with persistent state and a read-only model mount, verified its health/readiness/dashboard responses and ran pip compatibility checking. Model-job performance is still a separate pending measurement. Documented installation, API semantics, reproduction, upstream rights and current publication routes.

The full remote research CI passed. The minimal workflow exposed that the new preparation regression lacked the optional-Qiskit skip used by the other quantum tests. Corrected that dependency boundary and retained actual execution in the full suite; all 46 local tests pass. Prepared a deterministic, unjudged 40-edge graph worksheet so external semantic review can use source-grounded examples without mistaking automated extraction for verified factual relations. No human annotation result is invented.

Phase G completion — frozen outputs before interpretation

Finished all 18 primary configurations without changing their settings. Retained the one zero-feasible-shot failure and all failed cap diagnostics. Finished separate formulation, gate-cap and prepared-state controls. Audited 53,230 records across 24 grids, including independent tokenization/energy checks and recompilation of the gate-capped final circuits. All primary/formulation conditions use the same core source fingerprint; the prepared extension has a separate composite identity.

Generated full method tables, paired intervals, resource plots, token/corpus sensitivities and deterministic error examples. The principal sparsification comparison does not establish the intended evidence-guidance benefit. Kept the research framing comparative and diagnostic. No post-hoc noninferiority margin, winning-seed selection, physical-hardware claim or answer-based parameter adjustment was introduced.

Exported compressed public outcomes, common source snapshots and 110 frozen coefficient instances. Reconstructed all public tables without neural inference and reproduced four actual solver cases, matching selected IDs, full energies and line compilation. These checks complement the earlier exact restoration of all split/corpus files.

Phase H completion checks — actual execution beyond fixtures

Ran real CPU-container ingestion and five repeated three-selector comparisons. Verified cache reuse, local traces, persistent corpus retrieval and exact job-response survival after recreating the container on the same state volume. The single untrusted-source input was not selected into context, so it supplies no generator-resistance evidence. Browser visual review remains unavailable and is not represented as completed.

Profiled GPU embedding batches on 128 fixed development chunks, with three randomized repeats and synchronized timing. Verified the 240-token bound and vector agreement. Preserved the initial local timing export and published the final length-validated measurement. These operational profiles did not change scientific settings. Final manuscript export, page inspection and the versioned artifact package follow these checks.

Phase H manuscript export — inspect the rendered artifact

Completed the numerical manuscript and architecture/resource/sampling figures. Added explicit count/token, MILP, Ising, penalty and global-phase equations. Rendered the PDF, inspected all pages, widened method columns, kept figure captions and equation introductions with their content, and placed references on a dedicated page. Rebuilt and inspected the final 13-page export. Saved hashes and page-level QA evidence. This finishes the local manuscript/demo milestone; it does not claim external scientific approval, browser visual review or scholarly submission.

Phase I — package the measured state and preserve the handoff

Prepared a clean-commit release builder for source/configuration/evidence, the installable wheel, reviewed PDF and SHA-256 checksums. Added a claim-to-evidence map and an explicit list of external review, authorship, licensing, annotation and submission tasks. Added model-free public-table and original/prepared quantum reproduction commands to the full CI workflow. Kept the negative findings, local source archives and primary-versus-exploratory distinction intact.

The resulting artifact is a versioned research preview. It is not labeled as a submitted, accepted or independently validated paper. The local implementation, experiments, source restoration, statistical reconstruction, service checks and PDF inspection are complete within the recorded scope. No remaining human-only decision is represented as an automated result.

Documentation audit — reconcile explanations with the released implementation

Reviewed all three main documents against the plan, current modules, frozen configurations and saved evidence. Corrected stale present-tense baseline claims, expanded the current pipeline and data contracts, distinguished main-study JSON validation from the stricter baseline/service interfaces, and corrected the main encoder's batch size and MILP row counts. Added a current status table and explicit plan gaps while retaining checkpoint history.

Reconstructed all 24 public tables and paired intervals without loading models. Reran the intended test directory: 46 tests and 34 subtests passed. An initial unrestricted collection also discovered the extracted release's duplicate test modules under ignored results and failed collection; specifying tests avoids that local duplicate tree. No experiment, coefficient, reference annotation, model setting or frozen source was changed. The audit receipt records commands and scope. The existing release remains an immutable historical artifact; these documentation corrections are a later revision.

Post-release dashboard revision — design around the actual experiment

Inspected the requested visual reference and its styles, then replaced the original dark dashboard with a paper-and-blue laboratory design. Created an illustrative selection diagram, a clearer introduction, a frozen-study summary and explanations of the compared selectors. Preserved the distinction between simulation and hardware and between supplied sources and verified answer support.

Split the page into HTML, CSS and JavaScript; added a static asset route and wheel package data. Bundled the three fonts with their upstream licenses so the local interface needs no external font requests. Added editable source cards and a JSON view, source/count controls, keyboard tabs, explicit loading/error states, source-context inspection and accessible text for graph links. No research coefficient, solver, model or evaluation policy changed.

Verified nine DOM behavior groups, all 46 Python tests and 34 subtests, JavaScript syntax, Python lint, packaged wheel contents and byte-for-byte HTTP delivery of the page, styles, script and fonts. Updated the local container using the tested CPU runtime, retained its persistent state and preserved an old completed job response exactly. A real relevance/MILP/QAOA comparison returned India for all three without fallback. The old container is stopped and retained for rollback; unrelated services were untouched.

Chrome inventory was visible, but browser navigation and screenshot calls failed. The interface therefore has implemented responsive CSS and passing DOM/HTTP checks, while visual desktop/mobile review remains unverified. This limitation is explicit in the redesign receipt. The service guide documents the current interface and repeatable checks. The original research release remains unchanged.

Recoverable cleanup — preserve the study and retire the prototype

First inspected imports and documentation references, then tested a temporary tracked-tree copy without the prototype bundle. All 46 tests passed. Verified the system Trash by moving a disposable probe, restoring it without overwrite and returning it to Trash. Every subsequent removal used the same Trash mechanism; no Trash-emptying operation was performed.

Retired the original notebooks and standalone modules as one bundle, together with their obsolete requirements list and unused evaluation placeholder. The current first-baseline runner remains because tests and shared research contracts still use it. Replaced prototype links with release-tag links, consolidated the session-note observations into the report, and retained the original Word proposal in a private ignored archive. The original versions also remain in Git history. Updated the private learning-note reference without publishing that note.

Consolidated repeated Ising substitutions, sparsification-bound proofs, feasible-sampling calculations and bootstrap explanations in the technical companion. Kept its worked examples, assumptions and implementation checks. Moved generated build/cache outputs and disposable release/audit verification copies to Trash, while preserving full scientific runs, failed-run archives, datasets, weights and service state. A local recovery manifest records exact Trash locations and verified content hashes; shared documentation contains no machine-specific Trash paths.

Validation after actual retirement: 46 tests and 34 subtests passed; all 24 public statistical tables and intervals reconstructed; original and prepared QAOA reproductions matched; Python lint/format checks passed; documentation links and the unchanged scientific fingerprint were checked. The demo container had already stopped before this cleanup and was left in that state; no container or persistent volume was changed. The cleanup receipt separates this maintenance work from new scientific experiments.

Project journey — connect the explanations without changing the experiment

The presentation requirement was to explain the complete project inside the website while retaining the detailed source documents. Implemented a second page, /journey, and linked it from the existing laboratory. The reading sequence follows overview → current status → original plan → foundations → research design → baseline and phases A–I → results → reproduction → service → manuscript and external work. This preserves the distinction between historical implementation statements and current findings.

First established an explicit allowlist of public reference documents and numerical artifacts. Then wrote the chapter narrative and phase summaries, retaining the full selected source text in an in-site reader. Added local KaTeX equations, figures, source hashes and a deterministic generated bundle. Pinned development-only rendering/checking dependencies in a separate tool directory; service startup needs neither npm nor model weights for reading. The package-data configuration includes the generated content, fonts and figures.

Next added chapter/phase navigation, guided/deep modes, search, glossary, focus view, reference and artifact dialogs, keyboard behavior and responsive/reduced-motion rules. Mathematical interactions compute illustrative subset energies, MILP bounds, Ising energies, two-state quantum probabilities, sparsification bounds and sampling coverage. The results explorer reads saved analyses and explicitly preserves the original/prepared distinction and population/denominator limits. The live laboratory and research implementation remain available without replacing their solver policies.

Verification proceeds from source freshness and numerical identities to DOM behavior, actual HTTP serving with an engine that must remain cold, wheel contents and regression checks. CI rebuilds the generated bundle and detects stale content. Browser navigation and screenshot attempts failed in the available connection, so real desktop/mobile layout and focus behavior remain a separate unverified layer. The journey receipt records outcomes actually obtained; the build guide records maintenance commands. There is no new scientific result, modified frozen experiment or physical-device execution in this presentation revision.

Development sequence and implementation decisions

Version 1.4 working edition | Updated November 12 2026

This document records the progression from the exploratory prototype through the current research implementation. The first baseline was implemented during one November 4 session; its dependency-ordered account comes first. The November 10 phase entries then record the larger data, retrieval, optimization, quantum, service and research work. Early status tables are labeled historical and do not override later measured progress.

The [progress report](RESEARCH_PROGRESS_REPORT.md) records outcomes. [Technical foundations](TECHNICAL_FOUNDATIONS.md) supplies derivations and worked examples.

sections.title: Current state after the full local run
sections.text:
Current state after the full local run

This is the current summary. The stages and dated checkpoints below preserve what was true during implementation; their “remaining,” “next” and “pending” statements are historical unless repeated here.

| Phase | Implemented and executed | Remaining boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Measured environment, protocol, literature comparison, locks, manifests and CI | Exhaustive novelty certification and independent scientific review are not established. |
| B | Two frozen splits, annotation-preserving adapters, official metric checks and real empty/oracle diagnostics | Known contamination and annotation limitations remain. |
| C | Token-safe chunks, persistent embedding/graph caches, checked FAISS/SQLite index and retrieval/reranking policies | Cache and retrieval profiles are workload-specific, not general latency guarantees. |
| D | Signed count/token MILP, exhaustive checks, heuristics and entity-link features | Independent graph annotation and original-model closest-method reproduction are unfinished. |
| E | Actual QAOA simulations, mappings, sampling, noise diagnostic and full compilation | No physical quantum execution or quantum token-budget encoding. |
| F | Four hard-budget sparsifiers, development calibration and ablations | The proposed guidance benefit and preserved answer quality were not established. |
| G | 18 primary conditions plus six scoped controls, audited outcomes and reconstructed statistics | Small quantum subsets, shared generator family and non-certified large MILP cases limit generalization. |
| H | Numerical manuscript, reviewed 13-page PDF, real-model service/container checks and batch profiling | No independent causal error annotation, browser visual review or demo video; no production deployment claim. |
| I | Source/wheel/PDF/checksum preview release and reproduction instructions | Independent review, authorship/rights decisions, venue formatting and submission remain outstanding. |

There are 53,230 method/question records across 24 runs, covering 1,000 distinct held-out questions with methods, seeds and generators repeated. Of these records, 53,209 succeeded and 21 failed; failures remain in answer averages. The exact core source is preserved in [the scientific snapshot](research_report/evidence/scientific_source_snapshot.json). The [final audit](research_report/evidence/final_audit.json), [complete result index](RESEARCH_PROGRESS_REPORT.mdcomplete-result-index) and [claim map](CLAIM_EVIDENCE_MAP.md) connect status to evidence.

The [original-plan coverage assessment](RESEARCH_PROGRESS_REPORT.mdcoverage-of-the-original-plan-and-explicit-gaps) lists adaptations and unfinished requirements explicitly. Local phase completion is not literal completion of every original plan item, publication acceptance or completion of interactive learning exercises.

Stage two answer and evidence metrics

Added: [metrics.py](../src/qrag/metrics.py).

Answer exact match and token F1 are calculated separately from document precision, recall and complete-support coverage. Reference-normalization fixtures include repeated words, punctuation and special answers.

Why: document selection is an intermediate task. The project needs generated-answer measurements before claiming that a selection improvement benefits RAG.

Verification: offline metric fixtures and the later real generation run. Semantic near-matches and annotation inconsistencies remain visible in error analysis.

sections.title: Stage three a common objective and controlled classical selection
sections.text:
Stage three a common objective and controlled classical selection

Added: [optimization.py](../src/qrag/optimization.py).

SelectionProblem stores one linear vector and a strict upper-triangular interaction matrix. An exact-count constraint prevents the optimizer from improving recall merely by choosing more passages.

The module implements stable relevance top-k, MILP with product linearization, and a tiny exhaustive oracle. SelectionResult distinguishes ranking, optimal and limited outcomes and retains bounds when available.

Why: formulation and solver effects must be separable. A tested energy evaluator also gives the future quantum mapping a reference independent of circuit software.

Verification: MILP agrees with exhaustive enumeration on tiny positive/negative-pair cases and count boundaries. Tests also cover time-limited solutions without falsely labeling them optimal.

Remaining at this stage: native token constraints and additional classical baselines, subsequently implemented in Phase D.

sections.title: Stage four common real-model adapters
sections.text:
Stage four common real-model adapters

Added: [models.py](../src/qrag/models.py).

The model adapter resolves immutable MiniLM/Qwen snapshots, loads once, produces shared per-question features, constructs a consistent chat prompt and generates actual short answers. Embedding overlength and generation-prompt overflow fail explicitly by default.

Why: the compared selectors must use the same models and prompt policy. Model loading, feature generation and answer generation are distinct timing stages.

Remaining at this stage: chunking, persistent embedding reuse, hardware profiling and generation diagnostics with empty or oracle evidence, subsequently covered by Phases A–C and the final service/batching checks.

sections.title: Stage five experiment orchestration and artifact integrity
sections.text:
Stage five experiment orchestration and artifact integrity

Added: [runner](../src/qrag/experiments/run.py) and [artifact handling](../src/qrag/experiments/artifacts.py).

Each question is scored once; both methods consume the same candidate pool and features. Selected context uses original candidate order. Labels are applied only after selection/generation.

The runner saves manifests, question-level JSONL records and summaries. The manifest identifies data bytes, qrag source files, models, settings and runtime. Atomic writes and guarded resume prevent partial files and accidental mixing of incompatible runs.

Why: an aggregate result without the predictions and settings behind it cannot explain what changed or support a reproducibility check.

Historical runner boundary: completed error records are retained and skipped on resume. The later main-study journal retries errors with explicit attempt numbers while protecting successful keys. Failures before a run store exists may still have only a CLI error; not every possible startup failure produces a manifest.

sections.title: Stage six independent correctness and package checks
sections.text:
Stage six independent correctness and package checks

Added: [offline tests](../tests/test_baselines.py), an editable package and [CI configuration](../.github/workflows/baselines.yml).

The seventeen test methods exercise contracts and mathematics without downloading language models. An explicitly labeled fake backend tests orchestration; it is unavailable as an experimental CLI mode.

The package installed locally without downloads. No completed remote CI run was claimed at this stage; later phase entries record actual GitHub executions.

Why: a real model can produce plausible answers while masking a wrong objective or metric. Mathematical and interface checks need independent expected outcomes.

sections.title: Stage seven the real development run
sections.text:
Stage seven the real development run

Experiment date: November 4 2026. Run: baseline_dev_001.

MiniLM and Qwen ran locally on CPU with four PyTorch threads. There were three development questions and two methods per question. All six records succeeded with exactly five selected passages and no recorded embedding truncation or output-limit hit.

Both methods obtained answer EM/F1 of 0.3333. MILP obtained lower energy on each instance and higher average annotated document recall. Context-token consumption differed, so this was a fixed-count experiment rather than a token-matched comparison.

What this established: the complete baseline execution path works and exposes optimization, evidence and answer quality as different measurements.

What remains unestablished: general superiority, statistical significance, corpus-scale retrieval benefits, a novel graph method and a quantum advantage.

sections.title: Stage eight audit and objective documentation
sections.text:
Stage eight audit and objective documentation

Documentation and audit date: November 9 2026.

The saved objective energies and answer/evidence metrics were recomputed against the recorded coefficients and unchanged references. Dataset and qrag source hashes matched the saved run. The seventeen offline tests passed again.

One question had a semantic near-match rejected by token scoring. Another asked for a film but recorded a person as its answer; the earlier investigation located the same inconsistency in the cached upstream record. Neither primary label nor scoring rule was silently altered.

Added the objective progress report, compact evidence snapshot and detailed companion. No new model inference result is implied by this documentation work.

sections.title: Decisions and alternatives
sections.text:
Decisions and alternatives

| Decision | Reason | Consequence or limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Use supplied pools first | Isolates context selection | Does not evaluate corpus search |
| Separate labels in data objects | Reduces accidental answer leakage | Still requires split and contamination checks |
| Start with exact-count budgets | Removes passage-count imbalance | Token lengths remain unequal |
| Use native MILP count constraints | Gives a strong checkable classical reference | Quantum encodings still require separate work |
| Use continuous product auxiliaries | Exact with binary original variables | The continuous relaxation allows more points |
| Keep original context ordering | Controls a generation variable | Order sensitivity remains an experimental question |
| Fail overlong inputs visibly | Avoids hidden representation loss | Chunking is required for larger runs |
| Use JSON artifacts before tracking infrastructure | Keeps individual outcomes auditable | Rich experiment dashboards remain later work |
| Preserve problematic references in primary scoring | Avoids result-driven label changes | Annotation errors must be reported separately |

sections.text:
